name: lab_state
description: Read a network-xray lab state (read-only) and summarize it. Starts with `wrong`: what is wrong, each with a `text` line (an interface down, an OSPF interface that faces a neighbor and has no adjacency with the values both ends must share and do not, a Full adjacency whose ends still differ, a BGP session not Established, a route that cannot be used because its next hop is not reachable); empty when nothing is. only_problems: true returns only wrong and counts. Then nodes and interfaces, links, OSPF adjacencies, BGP sessions and counts. An adjacency that never came up is not in a neighbor table, so counts also has ospf_ifaces_expected (OSPF interfaces that face a neighbor, not passive), ospf_ifaces_full and ospf_ifaces_without_adjacency. No router is contacted.

path.description: The lab's state: an xray-states.js, a state_<node>.json, a folder of them, or a folder of saved FRR show ... json files, e.g. lab/xray-states.js

only_problems.description: true = return only wrong and counts (no nodes, links or adjacency lists). Default false

name: why_best_path
description: Quick look: for one node and an exact prefix, the BGP best path and only the reason stored in the data. For a step-by-step comparison of the candidates, or an address instead of a prefix, use why_path. Gives the BGP best path and the reason stored in the data (FRR selectionReason, or the IOS-XE collector's derived reason). If the data has no reason, reason is null and a note says so; nothing is guessed. A path with no local_pref gets a local_pref_note (the default applies; no value is filled in). Read-only.

prefix.description: Prefix, e.g. 8.8.8.0/24 (the length may be omitted when unambiguous)

vrf.description: VRF, only needed when the prefix is in several VRFs

name: list_routers
description: List the routers in a network-xray lab state and which protocols have state for each (ospf: OSPF neighbors or LSDB in the data; bgp: BGP neighbors or BGP routes), whether a routing table was collected, and row counts. Read-only.

path.description: The lab's state: an xray-states.js, a state_<node>.json, a folder of them, or a folder of saved FRR show ... json files, e.g. lab/xray-states.js

name: ospf_neighbors
description: List the OSPF neighbors each router has, as collected: for each neighbor its router ID, address, state (e.g. Full), interface, DR/BDR role and peer node name when known. All routers, or one with `router`. The answer starts with `wrong`: each problem for OSPF and interfaces with a `text` line (an interface down, an OSPF interface that faces a neighbor and has no adjacency, a Full adjacency whose ends still differ); empty when nothing is. To see why an adjacency is missing (the values both ends must share, such as MTU or hello), use ospf_interfaces. Read-only: answers from the state files, no router is contacted.

path.description: The lab's state: an xray-states.js, a state_<node>.json, a folder of them, or a folder of saved FRR show ... json files, e.g. lab/xray-states.js

router.description: Only this router, e.g. r1 (default: all routers)

name: ospf_interfaces
description: Starts with `wrong`: what is wrong, for OSPF and interfaces, each with a `text` line (an interface down, an OSPF interface that faces a neighbor and has no adjacency with the values both ends must share and do not, a Full adjacency whose ends still differ); empty when nothing is. Then `mismatches` and `hints` (below), then the OSPF interface values per router as collected: MTU, hello and dead intervals, network type, area, cost, DR/BDR role, priority, passive, authentication (none / simple / md5) and neighbor counts. For a link it also gives the other end and `mismatches`: one line per value that must be equal for an adjacency but is not, e.g. "r1 eth1 MTU 1500 ⇔ r2 eth1 MTU 1400". `mismatch_details` has the same lines as fields, with `odd_end`: the router whose value differs from its own other OSPF interfaces while the other end matches its own (an inference, with a `note`; null when that does not decide it, and for area). A value the router did not report is null and is not compared; each interface also has the neighbor state there, and `hints` names a link stuck in ExStart / Exchange whose MTU was not reported. All routers, or one with `router`. Read-only.

path.description: The lab's state: an xray-states.js, a state_<node>.json, a folder of them, or a folder of saved FRR show ... json files, e.g. lab/xray-states.js

router.description: Only this router, e.g. r1 (default: all routers)

name: bgp_neighbors
description: Starts with `wrong`: each BGP session that is not Established, with a `text` line (empty when none). Then BGP neighbors per router as collected: peer address, remote AS, iBGP/eBGP, state, established, and prefixes received (null when the data has no count). All routers, or one with `router`. Read-only.

path.description: The lab's state: an xray-states.js, a state_<node>.json, a folder of them, or a folder of saved FRR show ... json files, e.g. lab/xray-states.js

router.description: Only this router, e.g. r1 (default: all routers)

name: route_lookup
description: Look up a destination address in one router's collected routing table (installed rows only) by longest prefix match: the matching route, its protocol, next hop and outgoing interface (all next hops for ECMP). next_hop is null for a directly connected route; route is null with a note when nothing matches. A recursive next hop carries resolved_via (what the router resolved it through; via_mgmt when that is the lab's management network, i.e. not reachable inside the lab topology) and a note says so. When the data has the OSPF database (collected with network-xray 1.4 or later), the answer starts with `why`: one line per reason the destination has no OSPF route here or a different one (a router has it but does not advertise it, it is advertised by a router whose router ID another router also has, OSPF has the route but the routing table did not install it, a static route is not redistributed, an inter-area route). This reads the table the collector saved; it does not compute routing. Read-only.

path.description: The lab's state: an xray-states.js, a state_<node>.json, a folder of them, or a folder of saved FRR show ... json files, e.g. lab/xray-states.js

destination.description: IPv4 or IPv6 address, e.g. 8.8.8.8 or 2001:db8::1 (no prefix length)

vrf.description: VRF of the routing table rows to search (default: the default VRF)

name: why_path
description: Full answer (prefer this to why_best_path for "why" questions): it also takes an address, and when the router gives no reason it compares the candidates step by step. Why one router selected its BGP path to a prefix: the selected path, the other candidates with their attributes, the deciding step, and where that reason came from: reason_source "device" when the router reported it (FRR selectionReason), "derived" when the collector worked it out from what the router printed (Cisco IOS-XE prints no reason), "comparison" when network-xray inferred it by comparing the attributes in the data (Weight, LocPrf, AS-Path, Origin, MED, then eBGP over iBGP when the data says how each path was learned), or null with a note when neither says. summary gives the answer in one line; each path names the router its next hop belongs to (peer). A bare address is matched to the longest BGP prefix that contains it. Read-only.

path.description: The lab's state: an xray-states.js, a state_<node>.json, a folder of them, or a folder of saved FRR show ... json files, e.g. lab/xray-states.js

prefix.description: Prefix (e.g. 8.8.8.0/24) or an address inside it (e.g. 8.8.8.8)

vrf.description: VRF, only needed when the prefix is in several VRFs

name: state_diff
description: What changed from a baseline state you kept to the state now, heaviest first: routers gone or not read, interfaces down, OSPF adjacencies lost, OSPF interface values both ends must share that changed, BGP sessions down, best paths that moved (with the router's reason), routes removed or moved (with originated_by: the router where that prefix is directly connected), then what came back or was added. none is true when nothing changed. Uptimes, counters and the management network are not compared. The baseline is whatever path you pass as before (a state you saved, or collect's previous). Read-only.

before.description: The baseline state (same input as lab_state)

after.description: The state now (same input as lab_state)

mgmt_subnet.description: The lab's management network, left out (default 172.20.20.0/24; netlab: 192.168.121.0/24)

name: check_run
description: SolvedKit: is the lab solved now? Judges the lab's problem.json check against one state with the same rules as the page's Solved mark (one reading; the page also waits about 10 s for the check to keep holding). status is solved, not_solved, or cannot_judge (no check, or a router in the check is missing or cannot be read - then reason says which). results has one entry per condition (ok: true, false, or null when it cannot be judged). Read-only.

problem.description: The lab's problem.json, or the folder that has it

path.description: The state to judge (same input as lab_state)

name: check_verify
description: SolvedKit: does a problem.json check tell the broken lab from the solved one? status ok means the check fails on the broken state and holds on the solved state. Each condition gets a verdict: tells (fails on broken, holds on solved), both (holds on both - fine next to a condition that tells), wrong (fails on solved: the solved lab would never get the mark) or unknown (a router cannot be read). problems lists what to fix. Use it on a check you wrote before you publish the lab. Read-only.

problem.description: The lab's problem.json, or the folder that has it

broken.description: A state of the broken lab (same input as lab_state)

solved.description: A state of the solved lab (same input as lab_state)

name: check_suggest
description: SolvedKit: candidate problem.json check conditions from what the fix changed between a broken and a solved state of the same lab (the state_diff changes the check can see: a route now selected through an interface, a BGP best path, an OSPF adjacency Full, a BGP session Established, an interface up; the old best path kept as a backup). Every candidate is judged on both states; check is the proposed check, verified to fail on broken and hold on solved (status ok), or null with reason (status none; cannot_judge when the solved state cannot be read). A candidate marked binds_method names how a route is learned; it is not in the check unless nothing else tells (then warnings says so) - add it only if the problem asks for that. skipped lists the changes it did not use and why. It cannot know other ways to solve the problem. Read-only.

broken.description: A state of the broken lab (same input as lab_state)

solved.description: A state of the solved lab (same input as lab_state)

focus.description: The router to start from (default: the one the fix changed most)

prefix.description: The destination to start from, e.g. 8.8.8.0/24 (optional)

mgmt_subnet.description: The lab's management network, left out (default 172.20.20.0/24; netlab: 192.168.121.0/24)

name: check_init
description: SolvedKit: a problem.json draft for a lab from a broken and a solved state: format, focus, and the check from check_suggest; the title and problem text (English and Japanese) and the id are left empty for you to write (todo lists them). Returns the draft as problem; it writes no file. status none (with reason) when no check can be proposed. Read-only.

broken.description: A state of the broken lab (same input as lab_state)

solved.description: A state of the solved lab (same input as lab_state)

focus.description: The router to start from (default: the one the fix changed most)

prefix.description: The destination to start from, e.g. 8.8.8.0/24 (optional)

mgmt_subnet.description: The lab's management network, left out (default 172.20.20.0/24; netlab: 192.168.121.0/24)
